s: C. Judicial role and constitutional supremacy.
The Supremacy Clause (Art. VI, cl. 2) makes the Constitution, federal statutes made "in pursuance thereof," and treaties "the supreme Law of the Land," binding on state judges.
Marbury v. Madison (1803) drew the further inference that courts deciding cases must refuse to enforce statutes inconsistent with the Constitution.
A written constitution limiting legislative power would be pointless if the legislature could override it, and judges take an oath to support the Constitution.
Judicial review and judicial supremacy are different claims.
Judicial review is the power to disregard unconstitutional laws when deciding a case.
Judicial supremacy is the stronger claim that the Court's interpretations bind the other branches and the states generally.
Cooper v. Aaron (1958) asserted supremacy against Arkansas's resistance to Brown, and City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) invoked it against Congress.
Departmentalists (in the tradition of Jefferson, Jackson and Lincoln) argue each branch interprets the Constitution for itself.
Popular constitutionalists argue the people retain final authority.
Courts speak only in justiciable cases (Part II), only to the extent their remedial authority allows, and only on the questions presented.
In Trump v. CASA, Inc. (2025) the Court held that federal courts generally lack equitable authority to issue "universal" injunctions protecting non-parties.
